teaser: Sold for $200, refused by an art jury, hung in a hospital tent. Then it became priceless.
review_notes:
Sold to Jefferson Medical College in 1878 for $200; 2006 sale price $68 million, offer from the National Gallery of Art with the future Crystal Bridges Museum, matched by Philadelphia institutions; now co-owned by the Philadelphia Museum of Art and the Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts.
Centennial Exhibition 1876: rejected by the art jury, shown in the U.S. Army Post Hospital display.
Operation: removal of dead bone from the femur (osteomyelitis) of a young patient; anesthetic chloroform; anesthetist Dr. Joseph Hearn, probing surgeon Dr. James Barton, clerk Dr. Franklin West; identifications follow the standard literature.
Woman traditionally identified as the patient's mother (not documented by name).
Figures in the doorway: Gross's son Dr. Samuel W. Gross and the orderly Hughey O'Donnell (only the son is mentioned).
Eakins's self-portrait at the right edge, drawing: standard identification; very dark in this image.
Dimensions about 244 x 198 cm (8 ft x 6 ft 6 in). Gross was 70. Eakins was 31.
2010 conservation treatment correcting an earlier harsh cleaning.
Critic's reaction is paraphrased, not quoted.

lesson.text: $200. That is what Thomas Eakins was paid in 1878 for the largest and most ambitious picture he had ever made, a canvas taller than a door at about 244 by 198 centimeters, or 8 feet by 6 and a half. He was 31, and he had hoped it would make his name. It did, though not in the way he planned.

The setting is the surgical amphitheater of Jefferson Medical College in Philadelphia. Students sit in steep rows in the dark. Down in the pit, under a skylight, Dr. Samuel D. Gross, 70 years old and the most admired surgeon in the country, has just stepped back from the table to explain what he is doing.

Eakins knew this room. He had sat on those benches himself, studying anatomy alongside medical students because he believed a painter should understand the body from the inside. He painted the picture on his own initiative, with no buyer, for the great fair that would celebrate the hundredth birthday of the United States in 1876.

The operation shown was a modern one. The patient had a bone infection in the thigh. A generation earlier the usual answer was to cut the leg off. Gross instead opens the leg and removes only the dead piece of bone, so the patient keeps the limb.

Finding that patient is strangely hard. Eakins shows the body from an odd angle, cut off and wrapped, so your eye has to assemble it piece by piece. Start with the surgeon's hand and work your way across the table.

lesson.title: At the table
lesson.text: Four stops, from the scalpel to the anesthetic.

spots.title: The hand
spots.text: Gross's fingers are wet with bright red blood and hold a scalpel. In a picture made mostly of blacks and browns, this red is impossible to ignore. It is what shocked people most.

spots.title: The incision
spots.text: The cut in the left thigh is held open with metal hooks called retractors, while another surgeon probes inside. Eakins paints it as plainly as he paints a sleeve.

spots.title: The patient
spots.text: You see a bare thigh and hip, and below them feet in gray socks. That is nearly all. The patient lies on one side, legs toward you, head away.

spots.title: The white cloth
spots.text: A doctor presses a folded cloth soaked in chloroform over the patient's face. Anesthesia had been in use for only about thirty years. Without it, this slow, careful surgery could not exist.

lesson.text: Something else may have struck you. Nobody wears a gown, a mask or gloves. The surgeons operate in the dark wool coats they wore in the street, with bare hands. In 1875 the idea that invisible germs cause infection was still new and disputed in America, and Gross himself was not convinced.
The painting records a turning point. Surgery had learned to prevent pain and to save limbs, but had not yet learned to be clean.
Eakins could have painted all this as a neutral record. He did not. He lights it like a stage, and he gives the picture one figure who cannot bear to watch, placed where you cannot miss her.
See how light and geometry steer you around the room.

lines.label: The skylight
lines.text: Daylight drops from above, out of frame. It catches Gross's forehead and silver hair first, making his head the brightest point in the upper half of the canvas.

lines.label: Mind, feeling, flesh
lines.text: Three lit areas form a triangle: the surgeon's calm head, a woman's recoiling hands, the open wound. Thought, emotion and body, each in its own corner.

lines.label: Pen to scalpel
lines.text: A clerk writing notes, the hand with the blade, the incision. This slanting path links recording, teaching and cutting: the three jobs of a teaching clinic.

lesson.text: The woman in black on the left is usually thought to be the patient's mother. She twists away and claws at the air in front of her face. Next to her, Gross stands as still as a column. Eakins sets raw fear and trained calm side by side and lets you feel both.

The pose echoes a painting made more than two centuries earlier: Rembrandt's Anatomy Lesson of Dr. Tulp, in which a Dutch surgeon lectures over a body. There the body is a corpse. Eakins's patient is alive.

The jury choosing art for the 1876 Centennial Exhibition refused it. A portrait of a great American doctor was welcome, blood on his fingers was not. The canvas ended up in a model army hospital on the fairgrounds, hung among medical displays as if it were a piece of equipment.

Critics who did see it were torn. One New York writer admitted it was among the most powerful pictures of the century, then argued it should never hang where people with weak nerves might come across it. Eakins was stung, but he had left his mark on the canvas in more ways than one.
Eakins signed and dated the painting on a piece of furniture. Where?

spots.title: Eakins 1875
spots.text: The name is lettered on the end of the operating table, drawn in perspective as if carved into the wood. The painter puts his name on the surgeon's workbench.

lesson.text: He is also in the room. Tradition identifies the shadowy man at the far right edge, drawing with a pencil, as Eakins himself. He sits with the students, doing with his hand what Gross does with his: looking hard at a body and making precise marks.

spots.title: The painter
spots.text: Barely visible in the gloom at the edge, a seated man bends over a pad with a pencil. This is taken to be Eakins's self-portrait.

spots.title: Dr. Gross
spots.text: A high lit forehead, a halo of gray hair, eyes in shadow. He is not looking at the wound. He is thinking about what to say next.

spots.title: The woman
spots.text: Her face is hidden behind her arm. Her fingers are bent like hooks, the most violent gesture in the picture, and it belongs to someone who is only watching.

spots.title: The clerk
spots.text: At a desk behind Gross, a young doctor writes down the procedure. Every operation here was also a lesson and a record.

spots.title: The instruments
spots.text: Steel tools lie in open cases in the foreground, almost in your lap. Eakins puts you in the front row, closer than the students.

spots.title: The doorway
spots.text: Two men stand in the entrance tunnel. One of them is Gross's son, also a surgeon, leaning on the wall to watch his father.

spots.title: The students
spots.text: Rows of young men lean, slump and rest their chins on their hands. Some pay attention. Some look close to sleep.

lesson.text: Fourteen years later Eakins painted a second operating theater, The Agnew Clinic of 1889. In it the surgeons wear white gowns and a nurse stands by. Put the two pictures together and you can see medicine change.

Jefferson's alumni bought the canvas for those $200 and it hung at the college for more than a century. In 2006 the school agreed to sell it to museums outside the city for $68 million. Philadelphia was given a few weeks to match the price. Thousands of donors answered, and the picture stayed, owned today by two museums together.

quiz.question: What is Dr. Gross doing to the patient's leg?
options: Removing a piece of dead bone to save it
Setting a broken bone in plaster
quiz.explanation: He opens the thigh and takes out only the diseased bone, so the limb is kept.

quiz.question: Why do the surgeons wear ordinary dark coats and no gloves?
options: Germ theory was still new and disputed in America
Eakins did not want to paint white fabric
It was only a rehearsal on a model
quiz.explanation: In 1875 clean, sterile surgery had not yet been adopted.

quiz.question: What is the white cloth over the patient's face for?
options: To keep the light out of the eyes
quiz.explanation: A doctor holds a chloroform-soaked cloth there to keep the patient unconscious.

quiz.question: Where was the painting shown at the 1876 Centennial Exhibition?
options: In the main art gallery, in the place of honor
It was not shown at all
quiz.explanation: The art jury refused it, so it hung among medical displays.

quiz.question: Where did Eakins put his signature?
options: On the end of the operating table
quiz.explanation: His name and the date are lettered on the wooden table in perspective.

quiz.question: What happened when the painting was about to leave Philadelphia in 2006?
options: The sale was forbidden by a court
Donors raised the money to match the $68 million price
quiz.explanation: The city matched the offer and two Philadelphia museums now own it together.

facts.text: Eakins was paid $200 for The Gross Clinic.
facts.explanation: Jefferson's alumni bought it for that sum in 1878.

facts.text: The woman on the left is a nurse assisting the surgeons.
facts.explanation: She is usually thought to be the patient's mother, turning away in horror.

facts.text: Eakins had studied anatomy at the medical college where the scene takes place.
facts.explanation: He attended anatomy classes at Jefferson Medical College alongside medical students.
